title: KV cache deep dive - eviction/paging/long-context - Celerity Systems
summary: Deep technical troubleshooting session focused on KV cache eviction patterns seen in long-context workloads. Reviewed paging behavior, memory limits, prefix reuse impact on cache hit-rate, and mitigations (config tweaks, quantization, autoscaling of dedicated pools). Agreed to run controlled benchmarks, share kernel-level logs, and evaluate a short pilot with a dedicated pool plus adjusted cache knobs.
next_steps: Redwood: share kv-cache benchmark harness and recommended config (Priya)
Customer: run provided harness on staging and capture kv eviction logs (Jordan)
Schedule follow-up in 2 weeks for results review and pilot planning
action_items: Priya Anand: post kv-cache tuning doc + sample config (due: 2026-05-02)
Jordan Lee: collect eviction trace and heater logs from staging, upload to shared folder (due: 2026-05-04)
Alex Mercer: put together rough pricing for a 3-week Dedicated trial with 2 GPUs (due: 2026-05-01)
Maya Chen: open ticket with infra to enable extended KV metrics in staging (due: 2026-04-30)
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Rohit Sinha (Redwood), Jordan Lee (Celerity Head of ML Infra), Maya Chen (Celerity SRE), Oliver Park (CTO), Sara Voss (ML Eng)
---
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey all, thanks for carving time. The goal for today is a deep dive on the kv-cache eviction patterns you reported last week and try to pin down root cause and mitigations. Priya will lead the technical flow.
[00:15] Priya (SE): Hi everyone. Quick agenda: reproduce the eviction, talk paging vs eviction, prefix reuse effects, batching/throughput tradeoffs, and options (config, quant, dedicated). If at any point you want to jump to logs, Jordan sent a sample trace earlier.
[00:32] Jordan (Customer): Yep, I attached the trace and a short recording of the incident. TL;DR: periodic latency spikes and suddenly lower cache hit-rate when we cross ~8k token active sessions.
[01:05] Maya (SRE): To add — it's not just sessions, it seems when we have a set of long context conversations (30k tokens) plus lots of short ones, eviction happens and requests fall back to reloading KV pages, which kills p95.
[01:40] Priya: Cool. So first principle: our kv-cache is sized per-model and per-worker, with an LRU-style eviction and a paging layer when entries exceed memory thresholds. When memory pressure hits a threshold we page older entries to disk (or evict if paging disabled). Paging latency is high and explains the spikes.
[02:10] Jordan: One question — are we sure paging is disk IO and not remote KV service? Our infra uses an NFS mount for the cluster scratch, could that be the culprit?
[02:38] Priya: Good call. In hosted mode Redwood uses local NVMe swaps for paging; in Private/VPC it depends on config — if your staging uses NFS for ephemeral storage that will be much slower. That would definitely align with the high p95.
[03:05] Oliver (CTO): We are on your Private appliance in our VPC with a small local SSD but the nodes mount an NFS share for larger scratch. I believe paging fell back to NFS.
[03:32] Priya: That probably explains it. The eviction policy still evicts to the configured paging store. If paging store IO latency is high it will manifest as rehydrate pauses.
[03:50] Alex: Side note — we've seen prefix reuse patterns cause thundering rehydrates. If many concurrent requests reuse similar prefixes, the cache churn can amplify. Sara, you had an example?
[04:10] Sara (ML Eng): Yeah: a hundred web sessions share the same onboarding prompt prefix, but each then branches out. Because prefix is identical the cache warms with that prefix then evicts when unique tails cause collisions. We see repeated fetches for the same prefix but throttled due to eviction timing.
[04:42] Priya: Right. That's a classic: high prefix reuse increases effective working set for the KV cache because the shared prefix needs preserved entries for each conversation's unique continuation.
[05:05] Jordan: Is there a way to pin prefixes or increase their eviction priority?
[05:18] Priya: We don't recommend pinning in all cases; pinning reduces flexibility and raises memory needs. But you can configure prioritized residency for certain keys — in Dedicated modes it's a supported knob. For Private, we can enable a similar config but it's heavier on memory.
[05:45] Maya: Another data point: after enabling quantization in some tokens we saw memory footprint drop ~20% but p95 still spiked sometimes. Not sure if quantization is fully effective on the KV structures.
[06:10] Priya: Quantization helps model weights and runtime memory, but KV cache entries are typically embeddings/attention key-values that may not quantize well in the current pipeline. We have experiments with 8-bit KV packing, but it's experimental and can introduce small accuracy differences.
[06:35] Rohit (Redwood): We can share the 8-bit KV packing branch; it reduced footprint in internal tests but needs benchmark validation for your workload.
[06:50] Jordan: Please do. We can test but need to know the risk to output quality.
[07:00] Priya: We'll include a small eval set for quality checks.
---
[07:20] Priya: Ok let's look at the trace Jordan sent. (reads) At 12:14:48 we see a sustained increase in memory pressure and then a sequence of page-ins. The timing matches your reported p95 spike. The trace shows paging latency variances of 200ms to multiple seconds — consistent with NFS.
[08:05] Jordan: That 200ms baseline is already harmful. We expect sub-10ms for these rehydrates ideally.
[08:18] Priya: Exactly. For NVMe local the page-in is typically 5-20ms depending on size. So the first recommendation: ensure your paging store is local NVMe on the nodes (or an SSD-backed ephemeral) for any production long-context workloads.
[08:45] Maya: Noted — we can reconfigure staging to prefer local. In our Private setup the local disk is small; we rely on NFS for larger capacity.
[09:05] Priya: Then alternates are increase available RAM per worker (bigger instance), reduce per-worker concurrency to lower aggregate working set, or use Dedicated pools where the per-GPU memory footprint is increased and our runtime preserves more KV in memory.
[09:28] Alex: Also batching touches this. If you batch many requests, KV reuse increases but so does the working set. There's a tradeoff: bigger batching increases throughput and cost-efficiency but can push eviction.
[09:50] Sara: We noticed higher throughput times with 64 request batches. Reducing to 16 lowered p95 but increased token cost.
[10:12] Priya: That's expected. We can tune the continuous batching window and max_batch_size to balance latency vs costs. We'll provide suggested starting points for your mix.
---
[10:35] Priya: Next topic: prefix reuse and key collision. If you have many similar prefixes, the index structures can cause duplicate storage or eviction churn. Two mitigations: canonicalize prompts server-side to reduce duplicates, or enable compacted prefix sharing in the runtime which groups identical prefix KV across sessions. The latter is available in our newer runtime build but requires compatibility testing.
[11:20] Jordan: Is compacted prefix sharing safe for multi-tenant workloads? We worry about accidental leakage or side-effects.
[11:35] Priya: The sharing is within the same tenant/worker; no cross-tenant mixing. We also provide RBAC and audit logs. For Private deployments we can add explicit tenancy separation.
[11:50] Oliver: Good. We have strict tenancy rules.
---
[12:05] Maya: On the logs: we saw many small KV entries being evicted quickly. Could fragmentation be a factor?
[12:22] Priya: Possibly. Fragmentation of the KV arena occurs when lots of short-lived keys are created. Our runtime occasionally compacts but compaction is costy. You can reduce fragmentation by increasing TTL thresholds, decreasing churn (session pooling), or use our pooling feature that reuses KV slots for similar short-lived contexts.
[12:50] Jordan: TTL thresholds — what's safe?
[12:56] Priya: For long-context workloads we tune TTL to at least the average conversation length + slack. For example if average is 25k tokens keep TTL for 40k tokens or time-based TTL of 24 hours, depending on your retention needs.
[13:20] Sara: We have retention constraints for compliance — can't keep full contexts beyond certain time. That affects TTL choices.
[13:30] Priya: Understood. Time-based TTLs can be adjusted but we'll document options to balance compliance and performance.
---
[13:50] Priya: Now quick note on metrics: enable per-worker kv_cache_size, kv_page_in_ms, kv_eviction_count, and kv_prefix_hit_rate. Those will help us diagnose in future. Also capture system IO metrics for the paging device.
[14:20] Maya: We'll enable those in staging and forward to your support link.
[14:30] Alex: About Dedicated trial — we recommend a brief pilot with reserved capacity to see behavior under predictable host-local NVMe and increased memory. We'll sketch costs.
---
[14:50] Jordan: One more: we saw occasional mem spikes when quantized models loaded. Is there interplay between quant load and KV sizing?
[15:05] Priya: Loading different quant profiles can temporarily spike memory due to unpacking, indexing, or reformatting KV metadata. Sequence: load model -> allocate KV arena -> warm -> serve. If you rapidly switch models you can see transient pressure. We recommend model pinning for heavy long-context paths or using model variants in separate pools.
[15:40] Rohit: Also our runtime supports lazy materialization of some metadata to reduce peak spikes. It's off by default in stable builds but we can enable in a test branch.
[15:58] Jordan: We'll try that.
---
[16:10] Priya: Let's propose an action plan: 1) Ensure staging paging uses local NVMe or mimic hosted NVMe behavior; 2) enable the KV metrics and upload traces; 3) run our benchmark harness (we'll provide) with your long-context workload to replicate; 4) evaluate 8-bit KV packing and compacted prefix sharing in a test branch; 5) consider a short Dedicated trial.
[16:45] Alex: We'll also include a suggested config file with batching windows, TTLs, and priority residency knobs.
[17:00] Jordan: Sounds good. A couple of clarifying Qs: for compacted prefix sharing what's the expected memory improvement? rough ballpark?
[17:15] Priya: Ballpark depends on your prefix duplication ratio; if you have 60% identical prefixes across sessions compacting can reduce working set by 30-50%. We'll estimate once you share the prefix distribution sample.
[17:40] Sara: We'll export a sample distribution.
---
[18:00] Maya: Any security concerns with the experiment branches? We need the code to pass our SAST checks and we want change control.
[18:12] Priya: Understood — we can run the branches behind a feature flag in your Private cluster; code changes can be limited to runtime toggles. We'll also provide a short security summary for the feature.
[18:30] Alex: Competitors question — Jordan, you mentioned Anthropic earlier; are you evaluating them for this workload?
[18:40] Jordan: We're benchmarking multiple endpoints. Anthropic and OpenAI look good for short chat flows but they don't support our on-prem needs. You guys' private runtime is attractive if we can get predictable p95.
[18:55] Alex: Good to know. Ok last 28 minutes: we ran a short troubleshooting exercise live. Priya, remind the group what we did.
[19:10] Priya: We replayed the sample trace against a local NVMe-configured node and then against an NFS-backed node. The local NVMe run had stable p95 ~120ms, NFS had p95 spikes to multiple seconds. Also toggling batch size from 64->16 halved spike frequency.
[19:45] Jordan: That replicates what we see.
[20:00] Priya: We also instrumented the KV eviction counters; in NFS mode evictions/sec jumped 3x during the same load. That indicates page-in latency causing eviction cascades.
[20:20] Sara: Interesting. So the fix path is mostly infra + a few runtime knobs.
[20:28] Priya: Correct. The short-term path: move staging to local NVMe, reduce batch size, increase TTL. Medium-term: test 8-bit KV packing and compacted prefixes. Long-term: consider Dedicated pool or larger node sizes.
---
[21:00] Alex: Any blockers to executing these steps?
[21:05] Jordan: We need the harness and exact config examples. Also the security summary for branch testing.
[21:14] Alex: We'll send all that.
[21:20] Maya: Also please include exact metric names and a prometheus scrape snippet.
[21:28] Priya: Will do.
---
[21:35] Jordan: Quick note on cost — if we go Dedicated for a short trial, can you estimate token cost impact?
[21:45] Alex: Dedicated changes the unit economics; we'll estimate based on your throughput numbers. Rough initial estimate in the doc, final after you share workload.
[21:56] Priya: We'll also include guidance on autoscaling to avoid unnecessary cost during low-traffic periods.
---
[22:10] Alex: Ok let's recap and confirm owners. Priya will post kv-cache tuning doc and harness link; Jordan will run harness and upload traces; Maya will enable metrics; Alex will share Dedicated trial pricing; Rohit will coordinate experimental branches and quant packing artifact. We'll meet in ~2 weeks.
[22:40] Jordan: Thanks everyone. This was super helpful.
[22:45] Oliver: Appreciate the troubleshooting.
[22:50] Alex: Thanks team. We'll follow up with email and the artifacts.
[23:00] End of recording.
